CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1 · SEPTEMBER

Sine rule and cosine rule

How wide is the river if you cannot get across? How far is the ship from the lighthouse? In general triangles no right angle helps. Instead there are two rules that solve any triangle: the sine rule and the cosine rule. You learn when you need which.

8 LESSONS2 UNITSANY TRIANGLESURVEYING
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • set up the sine rule and rearrange it for a side or an angle
  • use the cosine rule as an extension of Pythagoras’ theorem
  • decide which rule fits the given parts
  • calculate distances to points that you cannot reach

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1The sine rule

In triangle $ABC$ draw the height $h_c$ from $C$ onto the side $c$. In the two right-angled part triangles $h_c = b \cdot \sin \alpha$ and $h_c = a \cdot \sin \beta$. So $b \cdot \sin \alpha = a \cdot \sin \beta$, and after dividing by both sine values $\dfrac{a}{\sin \alpha} = \dfrac{b}{\sin \beta}$. With another height the third side joins in.

KEY POINT · SINE RULE

In every triangle $\dfrac{a}{\sin \alpha} = \dfrac{b}{\sin \beta} = \dfrac{c}{\sin \gamma}$.

Each side stands above the sine of its opposite angle. You need one complete pair of a side and its opposite angle.

Fits for: two angles and one side, or two sides and the angle opposite the longer side.

Two solutions? $\sin \beta = 0.5$ holds for $30^\circ$ and for $150^\circ$. If the known angle lies opposite the longer side, only the acute solution is possible.

Largest angle, longest side: the largest angle always lies opposite the longest side.

INTERACTIVE · THE SINE RULE

Drag the vertices. The three quotients of a side and the sine of its opposite angle stay equal in every triangle.

EXAMPLE 1 · TWO ANGLES, ONE SIDE

Given: $a = 8$ cm, $\alpha = 40^\circ$, $\beta = 60^\circ$. Calculate $b$, $\gamma$ and $c$.

$b = \dfrac{8 \cdot \sin 60^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ} \approx$ 10.8 cm, $\;\gamma = 80^\circ$, $\;c = \dfrac{8 \cdot \sin 80^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ} \approx$ 12.3 cm.

EXAMPLE 2 · ACROSS THE RIVER

From $A$ and $B$ (100 m apart) the angles $65^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ to a tree $C$ on the other bank are measured. How far is $C$ from $A$?

Angle at $C$: $45^\circ$. $AC$ lies opposite the angle at $B$: $AC = \dfrac{100 \cdot \sin 70^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ} \approx$ 132.9 m.

EXERCISES

Given: $c = 12$ cm, $\alpha = 50^\circ$, $\gamma = 85^\circ$. Calculate $a$ and $b$.

$a = \tfrac{12 \cdot \sin 50^\circ}{\sin 85^\circ} \approx 9.2$ cm, $\beta = 45^\circ$, $b \approx 8.5$ cm.

Rearrange $\dfrac{a}{\sin \alpha} = \dfrac{b}{\sin \beta}$ for $\sin \beta$.

$\sin \beta = \dfrac{b \cdot \sin \alpha}{a}$

Given: $a = 7$ cm, $b = 5$ cm, $\alpha = 70^\circ$. Calculate $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $c$.

$\sin \beta = \tfrac{5 \cdot \sin 70^\circ}{7} \approx 0.671$, $\beta \approx 42.2^\circ$, $\gamma \approx 67.8^\circ$, $c \approx 6.9$ cm.

A ship sails straight ahead. At $A$ it sees a lighthouse at $32^\circ$ to its course, 5 km further on at $B$ at $58^\circ$. How far is it from the lighthouse at $B$?

The interior angle at $B$ is $180^\circ - 58^\circ$.

Angle at the lighthouse $26^\circ$. $BL = \tfrac{5 \cdot \sin 32^\circ}{\sin 26^\circ} \approx 6.0$ km.

Given: $b = 4$ cm, $c = 6$ cm, $\beta = 30^\circ$. Show that there are two triangles, and calculate both values of $\gamma$.

$\sin \gamma = \tfrac{6 \cdot 0.5}{4} = 0.75$: $\gamma \approx 48.6^\circ$ or $131.4^\circ$. Both fit, because $30^\circ + 131.4^\circ < 180^\circ$.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2The cosine rule

With the wooden strips the distance at $60^\circ$ is less than 5 dm, at $120^\circ$ more. So Pythagoras’ theorem needs a correction that depends on the angle. It is $-2ab \cdot \cos \gamma$: at $90^\circ$ the cosine is zero, for acute angles something is subtracted, for obtuse ones added.

KEY POINT · COSINE RULE

$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab \cdot \cos \gamma$, and correspondingly $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cdot \cos \alpha$ and $b^2 = a^2 + c^2 - 2ac \cdot \cos \beta$.

Rearranged for the angle: $\cos \gamma = \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$.

Fits for: three sides, or two sides and the included angle.

Negative cosine: if the calculation gives $\cos \gamma < 0$, the angle is obtuse. That is not a mistake.

Cosine greater than 1 or less than −1? Then the triangle does not exist: the sides violate the triangle inequality.

INTERACTIVE · THE COSINE RULE

Change the angle between $a$ and $b$. Watch the correction term compared with Pythagoras’ theorem.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE THIRD SIDE

Given: $b = 5$ cm, $c = 7$ cm, $\alpha = 60^\circ$. Calculate $a$.

$a^2 = 25 + 49 - 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 0.5 = 39$, so $a \approx 6.2$ cm.

EXAMPLE 4 · AN ANGLE FROM THREE SIDES

A triangle has the sides 3 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm. How large is its largest angle?

It lies opposite the 7 cm side: $\cos \gamma = \tfrac{9 + 25 - 49}{30} = -0.5$, so $\gamma = 120^\circ$.

EXERCISES

Given: $a = 8$ cm, $b = 11$ cm, $\gamma = 35^\circ$. Calculate $c$.

$c^2 \approx 185 - 144.2 = 40.8$, $c \approx 6.4$ cm.

A triangle has the sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Calculate the angle opposite the 7 cm side.

$\cos \gamma = \tfrac{25 + 36 - 49}{60} = 0.2$, $\gamma \approx 78.5^\circ$.

Two footpaths separate at an angle of $70^\circ$. Anna walks 3 km along one, Ben 4 km along the other. How far apart are they?

$d^2 = 9 + 16 - 24 \cdot \cos 70^\circ \approx 16.79$, $d \approx 4.1$ km.

A plane flies 200 km straight ahead, turns through $40^\circ$ and flies another 150 km. How far is it from the start?

In the triangle, the angle between the two stretches of the flight is $180^\circ - 40^\circ$.

$d^2 = 40{,}000 + 22{,}500 - 60{,}000 \cdot \cos 140^\circ \approx 108{,}463$, $d \approx 329.3$ km.

A parallelogram has the sides 6 cm and 4 cm and an angle of $60^\circ$. Calculate both diagonals.

Short: $e^2 = 36 + 16 - 48 \cdot 0.5 = 28$, $e \approx 5.3$ cm. Long (opposite $120^\circ$): $f^2 = 52 + 24 = 76$, $f \approx 8.7$ cm.

TEST YOURSELF!

$a^2$ from example 3 in cm²?

$25 + 49 - 35$

Angle from exercise 7, to one decimal place?

$\cos^{-1}(0.2)$

Distance between Anna and Ben, to one decimal place?

$\sqrt{16.79}$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Which rule fits? a) $a$, $b$, $\gamma$ given, $c$ wanted. b) $a$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ given, $b$ wanted. c) $a$, $b$, $c$ given, $\alpha$ wanted.

a) cosine rule   b) sine rule   c) cosine rule

Solve the triangle completely: $a = 10$ cm, $\alpha = 50^\circ$, $\beta = 70^\circ$.

$\gamma = 60^\circ$, $b = \tfrac{10 \cdot \sin 70^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} \approx 12.3$ cm, $c = \tfrac{10 \cdot \sin 60^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} \approx 11.3$ cm.

Two rafters, each 5 m long, meet at the ridge at an angle of $100^\circ$. How far apart are their lower ends?

$x^2 = 50 - 50 \cdot \cos 100^\circ \approx 58.7$, $x \approx 7.7$ m.

Connecting: use the cosine rule to show that a triangle with the sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm does not exist. What does the triangle inequality say about this?

$\cos \gamma = \tfrac{16 + 25 - 100}{40} = -1.475 < -1$: impossible. And $4 + 5 = 9 < 10$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY · SAXONY

With triangles across the whole of Saxony

Between 1862 and 1890 the Kingdom of Saxony was surveyed anew with a network of triangles. The work was led by the geodesist Christian August Nagel. On hills and towers there are still stone survey pillars today, from which the angles to the neighbouring points were measured.

Only a single distance of just under 9 km was measured directly on the ground: the baseline near Großenhain. All the other distances in the network were calculated from angles, triangle by triangle, with exactly the sine rule from this chapter.

Sources: Europäische Gradmessung und Triangulation im Königreich Sachsen 1862 bis 1890 (European arc measurement and triangulation in the Kingdom of Saxony 1862 to 1890), map document of the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin (kartdok); Staatsbetrieb Geobasisinformation und Vermessung Sachsen, annual report 2012.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

SINE RULE

$\dfrac{a}{\sin \alpha} = \dfrac{b}{\sin \beta} = \dfrac{c}{\sin \gamma}$

ASA, AAS, SsA

COSINE RULE

$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab \cdot \cos \gamma$

SSS, SAS

CAREFUL

$\sin \beta = 0.5$: $30^\circ$ or $150^\circ$

$\cos \gamma < 0$: obtuse

SPECIAL CASE

$\gamma = 90^\circ$: Pythagoras’ theorem

$\cos 90^\circ = 0$
